entry.title: Steering LLMs across cultures by listening to disagreement

link.title: Steering LLMs across cultures by listening to disagreement

entry.content:
A self-driving car’s brakes fail. It can swerve and hit two elderly pedestrians, or stay its course and hit two young ones. There is no factual answer to this. There is only a moral preference, and people don’t share one.

The Moral Machine, an online experiment run by MIT researchers, put dilemmas like this to people around the world and collected 40 million judgments across 233 countries. The answers differ by country: whether to favour the young over the old, the many over the few, the fit over the frail. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, don’t sit at a neutral point. Their default answers to such dilemmas land closest to those of Western, educated, industrialised, rich and democratic respondents.

Why does that matter? Because these models no longer just answer trivia. They already sit inside decisions that weigh one person’s interests against another’s. A content moderator asks a model whether a post mocking a religion should stay up. A hospital assistant helps a family decide how much risk an ageing parent should be allowed to take. A car designer asks how a vehicle should weigh the people it could harm. None of these has a factual answer; each rests on a moral preference. When an AI is in the loop, the preference it was trained on becomes the default, and the person on the receiving end never sees it and can’t change it.

“Aligning” a model means making it act on human values. But that goal only makes sense once we say whose values. A model aligned with one population is, by the same measure, misaligned with everyone else, and because a single model serves people all over the world, its defaults quietly apply one population’s values to billions of people who don’t share them.

The cost also falls unevenly. The countries furthest from the model’s defaults usually have the least data, computing power and access to AI companies needed to fix it. The gap is widest exactly where the means to close it are thinnest, so any fix has to work for them too. In our NeurIPS 2026 paper (Huynh et al., 2026) we ask how to close that gap using only what everyone has.

The constraint: an unchanged model and public survey data

Existing fixes each need something most users don’t have. Retraining the model on a country’s preferences needs preference data from that country and an expensive training run. Guiding the model’s output with a separate scoring model needs such a scoring model for every culture. Adjusting the model’s internal computations needs access inside the model, which commercial AI services don’t offer. The cheapest fix, simply instructing the model in the prompt, isn’t enough: describing a country’s values to the model barely changes its answers, and asking it to answer “as a typical citizen” helps but still rests on a single point of view.

So we work under a deliberately strict constraint. The model itself is never changed or retrained, there is no extra scoring model, and we never look inside it. The method also never sees the human answers we later use to evaluate it. The only country-specific input is the World Values Survey, a public survey that has asked representative samples of people in nearly 100 countries about their beliefs and values since 1981, from religion and family to trust and politics. And the only thing we read from the model is how strongly it prefers one answer option over the other.

Three observations

The design comes from three observations.

  1. A persona is a strong push, and too strong. A persona is an instruction such as “answer as a 30-year-old from Brazil”. Telling a model to answer as a person of a given age, income or religion shifts its moral decisions two to four times more than the same description shifts real people’s answers. A single persona overshoots, and it reflects whoever wrote the prompt more than the country as a whole.
  2. A country isn’t a single point. Survey data show that values within a country vary with generation and social position. A prompt describing one “typical citizen” throws that variation away.
  3. Pollsters solved this long ago. A pollster doesn’t trust one respondent. They ask many, report the average, and attach a margin of error. A difference smaller than the margin is treated as noise.

Put together, these change the question. Instead of asking how do we push the model toward a country?, we ask how far should any push be trusted? When the people we consult disagree, we should be careful about moving the model any further than their common ground.

Ask four local guides

Picture asking four local guides the way to the station. You walk in the direction their answers average out to. If the four agree closely, you also let them talk you through the last few turns. If they disagree, you stop at the average and don’t let any one of them talk you further.

Our method, DISCA (Disagreement-Informed Steering for Cultural Alignment), does exactly this with an unchanged model.

For each country we build four personas from the individual World Values Survey responses: one for each of three age groups (young, middle-aged and older adults) and one for the country as a whole. Each persona is a short paragraph, written in the country’s own language, describing values such as religiosity, trust in strangers and views on gender roles at the levels the survey measured for that group. The differences can be surprisingly small. The four US personas differ in just two sentences, about national pride and moral acceptability, and even that narrow spread carries useful information.

We then show the model the same dilemma once under each persona and read off how strongly it prefers each option. Two things come out of this panel of four answers:

  • The consensus, the average of the four answers, sets the direction. Moving the model’s answer to the consensus does most of the work.
  • The disagreement, how spread out the four answers are, decides whether to go a little further. Beyond the consensus, DISCA can take a small extra step chosen to suit all four personas. If the panel agrees, the extra step is kept. If the panel is split, the extra step fades away and the answer stays at the consensus.

Play with the panel

Below is one dilemma for one country. Each coloured dot is one persona’s answer: drag it left or right, or select it and use the arrow keys. The grey diamond in the top row is the model’s default answer, and the solid circle in the bottom row is where DISCA lands.

Disagreement
Extra step kept

The positions are illustrative, not measurements from a model. The extra step follows the paper's settings, explained in the next section, and is deliberately small: most of the movement comes from the consensus.

Two things to notice. First, the big move is from the model’s default to the panel’s consensus: four personas together pull the model far more reliably than any one of them could. Second, press “Panel splits”. The consensus barely changes, but the meter drops to almost nothing. When the people you consult disagree, DISCA doesn’t go beyond their common ground.

The whole problem is a game

How should DISCA choose that extra step? Step back, and steering a model toward a country turns out to be a negotiation. The four personas are the players, and each wants the model’s answer to land close to its own view. The model’s default answer is what happens if they reach no agreement. Any new answer is a proposed deal, and each player judges it by one question: does this leave me better or worse off than the default?

That is the setup of a bargaining game, the problem John Nash formalised in 1950 and Kalai and Smorodinsky later extended: parties with different interests looking for an agreement that each of them prefers to walking away. Game theory offers two classic ways to judge a deal:

  • Utilitarian: add up how much each player gains. This maximises the total, but it doesn’t care who wins and who loses, so a big gain for three players can paper over a big loss for the fourth.
  • Collective: judge the deal by how well it serves the group as a whole, which here means how well it respects the panel’s consensus.

DISCA scores each possible extra step with a blend of the two, leaning 70% toward the collective view. To do that, it needs one more ingredient: how a player actually feels about a gain compared with a loss.

Losing hurts more than winning helps

People don’t treat gains and losses symmetrically. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky showed that a loss feels roughly twice as strong as a gain of the same size: losing 100 dollars hurts more than finding 100 dollars feels good. This is called loss aversion, and their Prospect Theory captures it with a value curve that rises gently for gains and drops steeply for losses.

DISCA treats each persona as a loss-averse player, and that changes which deals win. Imagine a step that moves three personas a little closer to their views (+2 each) and pushes the fourth much further away (−3). A plain average calls it a good deal: (2 + 2 + 2 − 3) / 4 = +0.75. With loss aversion, the fourth persona’s −3 counts about 2.25 times as much, roughly −6.75, and the same deal scores (2 + 2 + 2 − 6.75) / 4 ≈ −0.2. It gets rejected. (This ignores the curve’s slight bend to keep the arithmetic simple.)

So among the small steps it could take beyond the consensus, DISCA favours the ones no persona strongly objects to. How much of that step it keeps still depends on how much the personas disagreed, as in the panel above. The consensus does most of the work; the negotiation only fine-tunes around it.

Does it work across the world?

We tested DISCA on 20 countries across four continents and seven publicly available models from five developers, ranging from small (2 billion parameters) to large (70 billion). Each dilemma is shown in the country’s own language, and the model’s answers are compared with how that country’s people answered in the Moral Machine experiment. Each cell below is one country and one model: blue where DISCA moved the model closer to what that country’s people chose, orange where it moved further away.

Hover over a cell for details. The colour shows how much closer to, or further from, the country's preferences DISCA moved the model, compared with where it started.

The grid is mostly blue, across every region and every model. It isn’t blue everywhere, and we show the orange cells on purpose: some country–model pairs get worse, and the smallest model gains the least. One comparison stands out. A 14-billion-parameter model with DISCA ended up closer to people’s preferences than a 70-billion-parameter model, five times its size, without it. The same approach also helps beyond car-crash dilemmas, on open-ended moral questions, questions about social norms, and free-form writing, though how much it helps depends on the task.

Limits

DISCA needs to read how strongly the model prefers each answer option, so it works with models that report these scores, not with ones that only return text. It also needs World Values Survey data for the country in question. And it doesn’t win everywhere: the orange cells above are real, and closing them is the next step.

The takeaway

Aligning a model with “human values” means aligning it with many different people at once. A panel of personas built from public survey data gives a cheap, honest way to hear them. And when they disagree, that disagreement is worth listening to: it tells the model how far it should go.

DISCA is a way to make a model less one-sided, not a claim that the majority is always right.
entry.summary: How a panel of personas built from public survey data, and the disagreement between them, can steer an LLM toward a country's moral preferences without retraining.

entry.title: Safety Game: teaching a black-box LLM when to say more, and when to say less

link.title: Safety Game: teaching a black-box LLM when to say more, and when to say less

entry.content:
Ask an AI assistant: “How do I create a strong chemical reaction at home?” It could answer in (at least) three ways:

  • Helpful but risky: “Mix household ammonia with bleach.” That is a real reaction, and it releases toxic chloramine gas.
  • Safe but useless: “You shouldn’t do chemistry at home, it’s dangerous.”
  • Helpful and safe: “Try baking soda and vinegar for a safe acid-base reaction. For anything stronger, use a supervised lab.”

We obviously want the third one. The hard part is that the assistant has no idea who is asking. The same question comes from a curious twelve-year-old, a science teacher, and occasionally someone who wants to hurt people. An answer that is perfect for one of them is dangerous for another.

Our ICML 2026 paper (Nguyen & Tran-Thanh, 2026) treats that uncertainty as what it really is: a game against an opponent whose intentions you can’t see. Taking the game seriously turns out to tell us exactly how an assistant should pick its answer.

The fix has to live outside the model

The usual way to make a model safer is to retrain it (fine-tuning, RLHF). That works, but it is expensive, and it has to be repeated whenever the safety rules change, whether because of new regulation, a new product, or a new market.

Most organisations can’t do this at all. A small company, a hospital or a public body typically reaches an LLM through an API: text goes in, text comes out, and the weights are locked away. Newer “inference-time” safety methods avoid retraining, but most still need to reach inside the model, for example to steer its hidden activations.

So we set ourselves a stricter goal: a safety layer that treats the LLM as a black box. It works with any model, needs no training, and can be switched to new rules on the day they change.

The spark: safe exploitation in poker

Poker-playing AI has faced a version of this problem for years. A strong poker bot starts from a solid baseline strategy that no opponent can beat by much. Against a weak opponent it could win more by adapting, e.g. bluffing more against someone who folds too often. But adapting is dangerous: the “weak” opponent might be setting a trap, and the adapted strategy might be much easier to exploit than the baseline.

Game theorists have a precise answer to this, known as safe exploitation or adaptation safety (Brown & Sandholm, 2017; Ge et al., 2024). Adapt all you like, as long as the adapted strategy is never more exploitable than your baseline. This line of work helped the Libratus bot beat top professionals at heads-up no-limit poker.

Our key observation is that an AI assistant is in the same position. Being more helpful than a flat refusal is a form of adapting to the user, and a user with bad intentions is exactly the kind of opponent who exploits it. So we carried the idea over one piece at a time:

In a poker gameIn the Safety Game
The opponent's hidden cardsThe user's hidden intent
A safe baseline strategyA safe refusal
The adapted strategyA mix of more helpful candidate answers
"No more exploitable than the baseline""No more than T extra risk compared with refusing"

The Safety Game

Here is the game. The LLM is one player and the user is the other. Before anything happens, chance decides what kind of user this is, and the LLM never gets to see the result:

  • Benign user. All that matters is how helpful the answer is. The LLM scores the helpfulness it gained over simply refusing.
  • Adversarial user, which happens with a probability set by a knob \(\beta\). What matters is risk. If the answer’s expected extra risk goes above a budget \(T\), the LLM pays a penalty.

Because the LLM cannot tell the two situations apart, it has to commit to one strategy that holds up in both. That is the defining feature of an imperfect-information game, and it is why the solution looks the way it does.

A strategy here means a probability distribution over a handful of candidate answers, with the refusal always among them. Just as a good poker player mixes bluffs with honest bets, the best strategy may be a mix, e.g. “give answer A 65% of the time and answer B 35% of the time”. Mixing lets the LLM hit the risk budget exactly, rather than falling back to the safest single answer below it.

To play, the LLM needs two numbers for each candidate: how helpful it is and how risky it is. In our experiments we simply ask the same model: “Does this answer the question well?” and “Is this potentially harmful?”, and read off how confident it is in yes vs. no. Models are often better at judging answers than at writing the perfect one from scratch, and any other scorer, such as a dedicated safety classifier, can be swapped in.

Play it yourself

Below are five candidate answers to the chemistry question, placed by how much extra risk they carry and how much more helpful they are than refusing. Drag the budget \(T\) to decide how much more exploitable than a refusal the assistant may be, and watch the game’s equilibrium strategy move.

The scores are illustrative, chosen to show the mechanics; they aren't measurements from a model. The dashed line is the best any strategy can do at each level of risk. A very loose budget lets even the bleach answer into the mix, which is exactly why T is the safety dial and is set conservatively in practice.

Try setting \(T = 0.20\) and ticking the comparison. A simple filter (“drop every answer riskier than \(T\), keep the most helpful”) is stuck with the baking-soda answer. The game can do better: it mixes baking soda with the slightly riskier elephant-toothpaste demo so that the average risk sits exactly at the budget. That freedom comes directly from the game’s rule, which bounds the risk of the whole strategy, as safe exploitation bounds the exploitability of a whole strategy, rather than judging each answer in isolation.

From a game to a tiny optimisation problem

Normally, solving a game is expensive. This one collapses into something very small: its equilibrium is the solution of a single linear program per prompt, with just a few variables. We solve it with an ordinary off-the-shelf solver that runs outside the LLM, so we never rely on the model’s own (unknown, possibly unreliable) reasoning to get the maths right. If no candidate beats refusing within the budget, the assistant refuses.

For the curious: the maths

Let the candidates be \(r_1, \dots, r_m\) plus a safe refusal \(r_s\). For each candidate, \(M_i\) is its helpfulness gain over the refusal and \(\Delta_i\) its extra risk over the refusal, so \(M_s = \Delta_s = 0\). With a strategy \(\pi\) over the candidates and the LLM’s penalty control \(\lambda \in [0, 1]\), the value of the Safety Game is

\[\max_{\pi} \min_{\lambda} \; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\beta+1} \sum_i \pi_i M_i}_{\text{benign user}} \; - \; \underbrace{\frac{\beta}{\beta+1} \, \lambda \Big( \sum_i \pi_i \Delta_i - T \Big)}_{\text{adversarial user}} .\]

For large enough \(\beta\) the inner minimisation simply enforces the budget, and the game reduces to the linear program

\[\max_{\pi \in \Delta^m} \; \sum_i \pi_i M_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_i \pi_i \Delta_i \le T .\]

The paper also proves the rule stays safe when the scores are noisy: if every risk score is off by at most \(\varepsilon\), tightening the budget to \(T - 2\varepsilon\) guarantees the true risk stays within \(T\).

Why the game matters

It would be easy to read the game as decoration on top of a reranking trick. It isn’t. The game is what tells us which rule to use, and each of the rule’s two key choices comes straight from safe exploitation:

  • Measure everything relative to refusing. In poker, you judge an adapted strategy by how much it gains, and how much more exploitable it gets, compared with the baseline. Here, every answer is scored by how much more helpful and how much riskier it is than a refusal, so the refusal is always the safe fallback.
  • Bound the risk of the whole strategy, not of each answer. Exploitability is a property of a whole strategy. In the same way, the budget limits the overall risk of the assistant’s mix of answers.

The second choice is what the obvious alternative, a simple filter that blocks every answer above a risk cutoff, can’t do. A borderline answer that the safety scorer is unsure about gets thrown away by a filter at any cutoff. The game can still use it, mixed with safer answers so that the overall risk stays within budget. In our experiments, these borderline answers were often ones that human reviewers judged safe, and recovering them is where the game’s advantage over filtering came from.

Limits, and the next game

Safety Game is only as good as its scores. When a model is too small to judge its own answers reliably, the game is playing with bad information; plugging in a stronger external scorer fixes this, because measuring and deciding are separate jobs. The budget \(T\) is currently tuned on a small development set for each task, and the game covers single question-answer exchanges, not whole conversations.

The game-theoretic view also points to what comes next:

  • Multi-turn games. Real conversations are sequential, and a careful adversary can spread a harmful request over several turns.
  • Multi-player Safety Games. A user, a developer and a regulator all have a stake in what the model says, and their goals differ. The same machinery can balance several players rather than one safety budget.
entry.summary: How an idea from poker-playing AI lets us make any LLM safer at inference time, with no retraining and no access to its weights.
